title: From the Editor — The Rookery
settingText: The Rookery as a sprawling frontier crossroads seen from slightly elevated distance: several roads converging, travelers and local workers moving through layered shade structures, carts, animals and worn machinery. Many distinct silhouettes without turning anyone into a mystical tableau.
summary: Art-directed opening editorial splash for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 10. Entice the reader, establish the live pressure and world feeling, and preserve the story page-one reveal.

panelPlan.text: SINGLE FULL-PAGE ART-DIRECTED SPLASH. Use one cinematic illustration rather than sequential panels. Reserve a large, deliberately quiet field for the supplied editorial body copy. The illustration supports the text without depicting the next issue's reveal literally.

LETTERING LAYOUT. Treat the supplied CAPTION lines as designed editorial typography, not speech balloons: strong heading, readable body copy, generous leading and margins, and a prominent final hook line. Do not invent any additional text, logos, signage, credits or slogans.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: FROM THE EDITOR

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: The road teaches one dangerous habit:

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Everywhere you go, everybody is new.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: New faces. New customs. New machines. New stories.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Spend long enough traveling and the unfamiliar starts to look significant simply because you were not there yesterday.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: The Rookery is where roads meet.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: People come in from everywhere.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: If the Sunfields are trying to assemble a pattern around Brandon Mack, this is exactly the kind of place you would expect to see it.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: It is also exactly the kind of place where you might fool yourself.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: — Jeff Hines

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Star Splitter Visions

title: The Rookery
summary: The group reaches the Rookery, a crowded crossroads where many distinctive travelers and locals naturally converge. Eva immediately starts seeing a pattern in the density of memorable people.

panelPlan.text: Wide Rookery: several roads converge through boarding rooms, markets, repair courtyards, animal pens and family workshops built around dark structural fragments.
Eva spots a masked herbal seller, a woman carrying red birds, an immaculate gambler, Dylan Sheets at a workbench and several other visually distinct people within moments.
Raina notices Eva counting and says nothing yet.
Brandon shoulders his bag through the crowd without receiving any special recognition.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Six people who look like they walked out of six different stories.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: That is called a town.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: At least wait until they do something unusual.

title: Marty Francis
summary: Marty Francis, the Rookery's perpetually busy host and social fixer, welcomes the travelers by asking the only questions he needs: names, debts and how long they plan to stay.

panelPlan.text: Marty approaches while carrying a parcel, settling a tab and directing a child toward the correct courtyard in the same continuous sequence.
He recognizes Jessie's vehicle model before he knows Jessie, then asks names without assigning histories.
Brandon gives his real name. Marty accepts it immediately.
Marty lays down the local rule of survival with dry efficiency.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: Names, how long you're staying, and whether anybody here is already angry with you.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: Brandon Mack. One night. Nobody I know of.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: Owe nobody money by sunset and we'll get along.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: How strict is that rule?

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: Strict enough that Dylan keeps eating here instead of collecting from me.

title: Stop Counting
summary: Eva continues categorizing memorable strangers. Jessie tells her to stop counting before unfamiliarity becomes evidence merely because she lacks context.

panelPlan.text: Marty walks Eva and Jessie through the first market courtyard while still performing errands.
Eva quietly marks visually distinctive people in her notebook.
Jessie catches the pattern and tells her to stop treating everybody new as a clue.
Marty asks what Eva is counting; she tells him about the recurring density of unusual people around Brandon and Sunforge remnants.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: Stop counting strangers.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: I'm checking whether the clustering is real.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: What clustering?

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: People who stand out.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: To whom?

title: Neral
summary: Eva's first striking stranger, a silver-masked herbal seller, turns out to be Marty's cousin Neral, whose mask comes from an old cooking burn and whose life is deeply local.

panelPlan.text: Eva points out the silver half-mask of an herbal seller in a shaded stall.
Marty greets him by a childhood nickname and asks after his daughter.
He explains Neral burned himself cooking mash twelve years earlier and has lived at the Rookery most of his life.
The visually mysterious mask becomes a known family history without making Neral visually ordinary.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: The silver mask.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: Neral. My cousin. Burned himself cooking mash twelve years ago.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: Does he always wear it?

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: Mostly because children like it and he enjoys being dramatic.

title: Tova's Birds
summary: The woman carrying red birds is Tova, a seasonal messenger whose birds are a practical route tool. Marty owes her money from a failed grain deal.

panelPlan.text: Eva points out bright red birds perched on a woman's shoulder frame.
Marty identifies Tova and immediately tries to change direction.
Tova intercepts him and reminds him of a debt in front of Jessie and Eva.
The birds launch to a nearby roof and return on command, demonstrating practical training rather than symbolism.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Red birds.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: Tova. Birds are hers. Debt is mine.

dialogueInline.speaker: Tova
dialogueInline.text: The debt remains mine until he pays it.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: Your welcome rule seems aspirational.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: It is how I know what to improve.

title: Dylan Sheets
summary: Dylan Sheets is another apparently mysterious figure who turns out to be at the Rookery because Marty owes him money and feeds him while pretending the debt is disputed.

panelPlan.text: Dylan works at a bench repairing buckles, stove hinges and hand tools with an artisan's concentration.
Eva asks why he came to the Rookery.
Dylan points at Marty without looking up.
Marty offers a competing account that collapses into a joke about food rather than hidden purpose.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Why are you here?

dialogueInline.speaker: Dylan
dialogueInline.text: Marty owes me money.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: Allegedly.

dialogueInline.speaker: Dylan
dialogueInline.text: He also feeds me.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: That explanation is disappointingly complete.

title: Learn Their Names
summary: Marty names the flaw in Eva's first pass: travelers see types because they meet people before learning the relationships that make them ordinary to one another.

panelPlan.text: From a balcony, Marty points down at people Eva initially categorized by appearance.
He names cousins, coworkers, ex-spouses, creditors and people who have returned seasonally for years.
Eva sees the same visually varied courtyard become socially connected once the relationships are supplied.
Marty tells her the first correction to a traveler's pattern is learning names before roles.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: They still look unusually distinct.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: You met a silver mask. I knew Neral when he had eyebrows.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: You're treating unfamiliarity as significance.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: Start by learning their names. The pattern can survive that if it is real.

title: A Broken Buckle
summary: Brandon and Dylan work side by side repairing a broken buckle from the rig. Their conversation begins with craft rather than mystery, allowing Dylan to approach the road stories indirectly.

panelPlan.text: Brandon brings a cracked leather buckle assembly from Jessie's rig to Dylan's bench.
Dylan makes Brandon hold tension on the strap while he replaces a metal pin.
They discuss the wear pattern and whether Jessie has been overloading one side of the rig.
Only after several panels of practical work does Dylan mention that Brandon's name is familiar.

dialogueInline.speaker: Dylan
dialogueInline.text: This failed because somebody keeps tightening it past sensible.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: Tell Jessie. I enjoy living.

dialogueInline.speaker: Dylan
dialogueInline.text: You sound more like Brandon than Brannock.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: That is encouraging.

title: The Man With Many Names
summary: Dylan has heard the road story of a black-coated man who is Brannock in one town, a general in another and Merritt somewhere else. The separate identity stories are beginning to merge into one legend.

panelPlan.text: Dylan fits the new buckle pin while describing versions of the story heard from different travelers.
One version makes Brannock a former general; another says Merritt and Brannock are aliases used by the same outlaw.
Eva hears the names combine in ways no original community believed.
Brandon points to the process as proof that provenance will become harder to reconstruct over time.

dialogueInline.speaker: Dylan
dialogueInline.text: The road says Brannock used to be a general.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: The road ought to pick one.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: It is mixing the names together now.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: Stories do that when the next teller likes the larger version.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: Then the next town can repeat anything and call it memory.

title: Tomas Says Brandon
summary: Dylan knows Brandon's actual name because Tomas at the Last Drop has been deliberately correcting travelers, creating a counter-rumor that moves through the same social channels as Brannock.

panelPlan.text: Dylan says he heard the name Brandon from a wagon crew that stopped at the Last Drop.
According to them, Tomas interrupts Brannock stories to identify Brandon Mack as the man who cut him down.
Eva realizes accurate correction can travel too, though it competes with the more dramatic legend.
Brandon smiles despite himself at Tomas doing useful work after he left.

dialogueInline.speaker: Dylan
dialogueInline.text: Tomas says you're Brandon Mack.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: Tomas is doing useful work.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: So the real name is traveling too.

dialogueInline.speaker: Dylan
dialogueInline.text: It is less entertaining. That slows it down.

title: Provenance Gets Harder
summary: Eva and Raina confront a methodological problem: once identity stories merge on the road, a future wrong name may be impossible to classify as new evidence, ordinary gossip or contamination from older cases.

panelPlan.text: Eva brings Dylan's merged rumor to Raina at a courtyard table.
Raina marks all future identity reports as provenance-sensitive rather than independent by default.
Brandon points out that this is another reason not to treat every wrong name as proof of a deeper force.
Eva dislikes losing a clean measurement but accepts the contamination.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: If the names are merging, the next one might come from the old stories.

dialogueInline.speaker: Raina
dialogueInline.text: Then a new report is not independent unless we can trace it.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: Which means fewer reasons to chase every rumor.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: You are enjoying that conclusion too much.

title: Three Black Things
summary: Raina turns from people to the Rookery's dark structural remnants and initially classifies three visible objects as Sunforge fragments because of material and form.

panelPlan.text: Raina sketches three objects: a black roof support, a half-buried curved form near the pens and a low dark bench-like slab.
She notes similar surface material, heat behavior and ribbed geometry.
Marty watches her confidently group them and asks what evidence says they share one history.
Jessie recognizes the same category problem Saint Oren's exposed.

dialogueInline.speaker: Raina
dialogueInline.text: Three structures. Same material family.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: You moved from material to family quickly.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: What do you call them?

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: Three different things.

title: The Roof Brace
summary: The roof support has a documented local history: Marty's grandfather hauled it from a collapsed structure miles away because the material was strong and heat-resistant.

panelPlan.text: Marty leads them to the black roof support built into a crowded workshop.
Old bolt holes and mismatched masonry make clear it was installed long after the building was erected.
Marty says his grandfather hauled it here with six animals after a storm exposed material along another route.
Raina notes that whatever the object's origin, its current location tells them nothing about where it was first embedded.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: My grandfather dragged this in from East Wash.

dialogueInline.speaker: Raina
dialogueInline.text: Then it is displaced material.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: It is a roof brace. Displaced material is your problem.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Both descriptions can be true.

title: The Old Black Thing
summary: The half-buried object has the opposite history: nobody remembers it arriving. The settlement grew around it, and locals know more about its practical effects than its origin.

panelPlan.text: Near the pens, a black curved form emerges from pale ground and serves as a windbreak.
Marty says the oldest stories already place it there; nobody alive knows its full shape underground.
Locals avoid driving stakes near one side because the ground is hard and shallow over buried material.
Raina records a distinct provenance class rather than merging it with the roof brace.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: That one was here before the first Francis built a wall.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: Nobody tried to dig it out?

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: People have better ways to spend a week than losing shovels.

dialogueInline.speaker: Raina
dialogueInline.text: Different history. Similar material.

title: The Bench Everybody Hates
summary: The third object was salvaged elsewhere and repurposed as a bench that becomes unpleasantly hot. Its mundane local reputation punctures the travelers' instinct to treat dark material as sacred or ominous.

panelPlan.text: Marty brings them to a low black slab under partial shade. Nobody is sitting on it.
Eva asks why the bench is empty despite a crowded courtyard.
Jessie touches the edge and immediately pulls her hand away from stored heat.
Marty says an uncle salvaged it from south of the Rookery and regrets turning it into furniture.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Why does everybody hate the bench?

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: It gets hot.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: That is an aggressively complete explanation.

dialogueInline.speaker: Raina
dialogueInline.text: And another displaced object.

title: One Traveler Word
summary: Eva recognizes that 'Sunforge' may be a useful traveler category that obscures distinct histories. Raina keeps the material correlation but stops treating the word as an established scientific class.

panelPlan.text: The four sit in shade with Raina's three sketches arranged separately rather than grouped.
Eva writes the local histories beside each object instead of one shared label.
Marty says travelers need broad terms because they cross places quickly; residents need distinctions because they live with consequences.
Raina leaves 'Sunforge?' as a question in her notes rather than an answer.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: We use one word because we see them across the road.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: And we use three histories because we live with them.

dialogueInline.speaker: Raina
dialogueInline.text: The shared material still matters.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: It can matter without settling what the things are.

title: Something Interesting
summary: Eva notices several travelers independently saying they came to the Rookery because they heard 'something interesting' was happening. The phrase looks like a convergence signal until Marty asks where each person heard it.

panelPlan.text: At supper, a traveler mentions hearing something interesting was happening at the Rookery.
Eva asks two others and gets variations of the same phrase.
Raina becomes alert because no one in their group seeded it.
Marty turns the question around and begins asking for sources.

dialogueInline.speaker: Traveler
dialogueInline.text: I heard something interesting was happening here.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Who told you?

dialogueInline.speaker: Traveler
dialogueInline.text: Mary at South Cut.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: Mary got it from Len.

dialogueInline.speaker: Samuel
dialogueInline.text: Len told me he heard it from Bellweather.

title: After Supper
summary: The group traces the rumor around the supper tables and finds multiple mundane motives for coming to the Rookery: a card game, cheap beds, a buyer, a funeral, debt collection and ordinary family visits.

panelPlan.text: Marty insists they eat before turning supper into an interrogation.
Afterward, Eva and Raina ask travelers why they came and who mentioned the Rookery.
Reasons overlap without matching: Dylan came for debt and food, another traveler for a rumored buyer, another for a funeral, another because cousins live here.
The phrase 'something interesting' is attached after the fact to many different practical trips.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: Investigate after supper. I refuse to let a theory cool the beans.

dialogueInline.speaker: Dylan
dialogueInline.text: I came because Marty owes me money.

dialogueInline.speaker: Traveler
dialogueInline.text: I heard there was a buyer for glass wire.

dialogueInline.speaker: Second Traveler
dialogueInline.text: My cousin said the rooms were cheap this week.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: The mystery is becoming affordable lodging.

title: The Loop
summary: Raina attempts to trace 'something interesting' backward and encounters a social loop: people cite one another, repeat phrases without remembering the first speaker and attach them to unrelated reasons for travel.

panelPlan.text: Raina draws a simple chain of names from Mary to Len to Bellweather to another traveler and back toward a South Cut wagon crew.
At least one source is secondhand from somebody who heard the phrase after already deciding to travel.
Samuel recognizes the same social aggregation he exploited deliberately, this time apparently happening without a mastermind.
Marty predicts the chain will eventually terminate in a cousin who cannot remember who started it.

dialogueInline.speaker: Raina
dialogueInline.text: Everybody knows the last person in the chain, not the first.

dialogueInline.speaker: Samuel
dialogueInline.text: Expectation can aggregate without anyone planning it.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Can we walk it backward?

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: You can try. You will end up at somebody's cousin.

title: A Crowd Without a Cause
summary: Samuel distinguishes the Rookery convergence from his earlier manipulation. The social mechanism is similar, but here ordinary rumor, economics and travel routes are sufficient to concentrate people without a hidden organizer.

panelPlan.text: Samuel compares the rumor loop to his own planted stories without claiming innocence.
He explains that his method worked because communities already do this naturally; he only inserted a particularly effective seed.
Raina marks the current convergence as explained enough not to use as evidence of an external force.
Eva accepts the downgrade while keeping the unresolved Rider and Hushwater-style future possibilities separate.

dialogueInline.speaker: Samuel
dialogueInline.text: I did not invent the mechanism. I exploited it.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: Which means seeing the mechanism is not proof somebody is exploiting it now.

dialogueInline.speaker: Raina
dialogueInline.text: This convergence is explainable without an organizer.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Then it comes off the mystery board.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: I am relieved to have escaped a board I never agreed to join.

title: Constellations
summary: From a high gallery, Marty shows how travelers manufacture constellations from people whose connections they cannot see. Raina accepts the correction without pretending it explains every recurrence elsewhere.

panelPlan.text: At dusk on a high gallery, Marty points down at Neral, Tova, Dylan and several others Eva had originally marked as distinct oddities.
He narrates the ordinary ties between them: family, work, debt, marriage, history and routine.
Raina closes one notebook containing the Rookery convergence but keeps another with Brannock, Merritt, the blue-room phrase and the Rider.
Eva asks whether every strange person becomes ordinary once you know enough. Marty refuses the reverse simplification too.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: You saw six separate stories because you arrived yesterday.

dialogueInline.speaker: Raina
dialogueInline.text: That does not explain every recurrence we have seen.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: I did not say it did.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Maybe everybody looks strange until you know the history.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: And sometimes the history stays strange.

title: Three Histories, Not One
summary: The group leaves the Rookery with a refined method: learn local histories before treating repeated visual forms, unusual people or rumor convergence as one phenomenon. The next road leads toward Glasshouse.

panelPlan.text: Morning departure from the Rookery. Marty collects the remaining room debt and points Jessie toward the road to Glasshouse.
Raina's notes now separate local explanations from unresolved cases instead of forcing a unified category.
Eva says the Rookery made the mystery smaller in a useful way.
Brandon looks satisfied by any conclusion that removes him from the center, while Jessie notices the Glasshouse road with private recognition she does not explain yet.

dialogueInline.speaker: Marty Francis
dialogueInline.text: You came looking for one pattern and found several histories.

dialogueInline.speaker: Raina
dialogueInline.text: That is better.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Smaller mysteries are easier to carry.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: Pack lightly.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: Glasshouse is a day's drive if the west road holds.

title: Next: WHAT JESSIE LEFT
settingText: Glasshouse courtyard viewed from the road. One figure has turned toward an unseen voice from inside while another road continues out of frame. Keep faces unreadable and identities unconfirmed.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: They have spent months asking what kind of story Brandon belongs to.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: At Glasshouse, somebody knows exactly what story Jessie left.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: She gets the name right.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: She gets the history right.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: And Jessie, for once, is the one looking toward the road.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: NEXT: WHAT JESSIE LEFT
